title: Technology leadership, close to the work.
role: Technology leader · Full-stack engineer · Customer success
summary: A career connecting product delivery, engineering, and customer success with the systems a business depends on every day.
brief: The opening slide brings together three perspectives: directing technology, building software, and helping customers succeed. The work that follows spans wine ecommerce, financial-services software, cloud infrastructure, telecommunications, government publishing, hospitality, and news media.
ownership: Connect business requirements with practical engineering and delivery decisions.
Coordinate developers, operations teams, vendors, and business stakeholders.
Stay involved through implementation, launch, support, and adoption.
delivery: The commercial work ranges from large historical order migrations to customer onboarding and public-facing publishing. Across these settings, delivery involves both the software and the people who operate it: clear specifications, coordinated releases, useful documentation, and ownership after launch.

Independent work adds a founder’s perspective. Citizen Success combines a political geography database, publishing, subscriptions, payments, and self-hosted operations. The introductory slide also lists cultural projects, sustainability studies, and open-source event organizing; these are background interests rather than separate project slides in this PDF.
outcomes: A portfolio that shows both hands-on implementation and cross-functional leadership.
Dedicated examples of commerce modernization, technical customer success, operational delivery, and publishing.
lesson: Technology leadership is most useful when strategy, implementation, and operating responsibility stay connected. These case studies show how I work across those boundaries.

title: Modernizing commerce at scale.
summary: Migrated historical commerce data to Shopify and Linnworks while working across platform operations, internal tools, performance, and IT for a growing wine business.
brief: A Napa-based wine ecommerce group was moving from the legacy Offset Figure inventory and commerce platform to Shopify and Linnworks. The modernization sat within a broader growth environment involving organic expansion, private equity, and acquisitions. My role expanded from ecommerce administration to Director of Technology.
ownership: Develop the Python and Pandas workflows used to migrate historical order and customer data.
Work across strategy, implementation, and daily operations for the commerce platforms.
Support internal tools, web performance, Cloudflare security, and corporate IT.
delivery: I authored Python and Pandas notebooks for the order and customer migration, using SQL alongside the new commerce and warehouse systems. The historical transfer covered two million orders representing $150 million in order value. These totals refer to historical orders transferred between platforms.

The operating environment included Shopify Plus, Linnworks, Klaviyo, and AfterShip. Retool work connected internal-tool development with QA, user acceptance, and deployment. BrowserStack and Datadog supported performance work; Cloudflare WAF, bot controls, and Workers formed part of the web infrastructure. Linux, Docker Compose, and Airbyte were also part of the broader technical environment.
outcomes: Completed the documented migration of two million historical orders and their associated order value.
Established production operations across the new commerce, warehouse, marketing, and post-purchase stack.
Supported a business reporting 40% group-wide growth through technology modernization and operating delivery.
lesson: A commerce migration is also an operations project. Historical data, warehouse workflows, internal tooling, performance, and business ownership all need to move together.
note: The 40% figure is group-wide business growth, not an isolated attribution to this migration. The measurement period is not specified here.

title: From connected risks to a practical next step.
image_alt: Digital Younger Dryas artwork for Cyberpolycrisis: a man and woolly mammoth crossing a snowy landscape toward sunrise
summary: Built a Cloudflare-hosted product that connects cyber research, public website checks, an AI assistant, and a guided health review to help businesses decide what to investigate and improve next.
brief: A business owner can read about a breach or supplier outage without knowing what it means for tomorrow’s orders, staff, or customer commitments. Cyberpolycrisis turns that information gap into a product journey: understand the relevant dependencies, ask questions in context, and leave with an action plan. I developed the research, product experience, application, and Cloudflare deployment as one connected service.
ownership: Define the journey from a public website check or research article into a conversation, a structured review, and practical next steps.
Develop the report library, role-specific guidance, visual identity, and Digital Younger Dryas storytelling.
Build the frontend, Workers APIs, AI retrieval, questionnaire model, optional follow-up storage, and deployment workflow.
Design request limits, verification, privacy choices, and mobile behavior as part of the product experience.
delivery: The entry point asks visitors to add their website. After Cloudflare Turnstile verification, bounded checks examine public DNS screening, the HTTPS homepage response, selected security headers, and visible platform signals. Signed observations then open a conversation with Ask Cyberpolycrisis. These observations provide context; they do not establish compromise, installed software versions, or a complete vulnerability assessment.

The assistant runs on Cloudflare Workers AI with a curated, locally bundled retrieval index. It retrieves relevant research by topic and audience, and provides links back to the underlying material. The library expands the original 26 topics into ten detailed reports each, with guidance for business owners, business managers, technology managers, software engineers, customer-service staff, and customers. A downloadable 31-page report and a dated 28-topic register provide additional entry points.

The Cyber Health Review covers twelve controls across identity, software, AI, data, network trust, and recovery. A deterministic model turns self-reported answers into a readiness view, an overlapping-risk map, and prioritized actions. Platform options—including Shopify, Palantir, Cloudflare, and Databricks—are matched to business requirements and retained responsibilities, rather than presented as guarantees of safety.

The chat-to-review handoff minimizes the conversation without discarding its in-memory session. Mobile work addressed iPhone viewport height, keyboard space, verification delays, readable response scrolling, and reopening chat. The Digital Younger Dryas identity uses eight rotating scenes, swipe controls, and reduced-motion behavior to connect the research with a recognizable visual story.

The backend separates model advice from application authority. The assistant cannot execute tools or fetch arbitrary sites; the dedicated website-check endpoint validates public destinations and bounds redirects, response sizes, and time. Server-side verification, rate limits, and a Durable Object inference budget constrain abuse. Questionnaire answers remain local unless explicitly shared with chat, while optional follow-up requests store only consent and contact details in D1 for a manual response.
outcomes: Published a working product on cyberpolycrisis.com, connecting research, website onboarding, AI conversation, and the Cyber Health Review.
Delivered 260 detailed reports across the original 26 topics, with six audience perspectives and a shared retrieval corpus for the assistant.
Implemented an action-plan workflow with a connected-risk visualization, platform evaluation, local exports, and an explicit path to human follow-up.
Verified the live website-check-to-chat handoff and conversation-preserving review navigation, alongside automated checks for request boundaries and interaction state.
note: The research is a dated snapshot, with an evidence cutoff of 22 October 2026. The review is a planning tool and the public website checks are a starting point, not a security audit. These results describe delivered capabilities; no customer adoption, revenue impact, or reduction in security incidents is claimed.
lesson: An AI product becomes useful when it connects a person’s question to evidence, a bounded workflow, and an accountable next action. The conversation, controls, and operating model need to be designed together.

title: Public data, built into a working product.
summary: Built a political geography and publishing platform combining searchable public data, subscriptions, payments, real-time discussion, and self-hosted infrastructure.
brief: Citizen Success brought a political geography database and a subscription publishing product into the same application. The data model covered parties, politicians, states, legislative chambers, and divisions. The product also needed content creation, access permissions, payments, and interactive conversations.
ownership: Build the application and the public-data search experience.
Connect publishing, subscriptions, permissions, and payment integrations.
Operate the deployment, database, storage, email, and backup environment.
delivery: Phoenix LiveView powered reactive filtering and real-time post chat. Channels, posts, custom page layouts, a rich-text editor, and S3 uploads supported the publishing workflow. React and Svelte components were integrated into LiveView where needed, while a theming engine supported multiple sites and domains.

The implementation connected Stripe through JSON/REST and Authorize.Net through XML. A permission system expressed access in terms of users, powers, actions, and schemas. The self-hosted environment used Debian, Ansible, PostgreSQL, and Docker Compose, with Wasabi S3 storage, Cloudflare CDN, and geographically redundant backup arrangements.
outcomes: Delivered a searchable political database and publishing application in one product.
Provided political database queries and lists to campaigns.
Built the operational foundation for multiple sites, subscriptions, and real-time content interactions.
lesson: Founder-led product engineering includes the less visible work: permissions, backups, publishing operations, and maintainable integrations. Those capabilities make the visible product usable in practice.
image_alt: Citizen Success portfolio slide with political database filters and publishing interface screenshots

title: Turning data platforms into customer adoption.
summary: Led engineering delivery and customer engagement across data-driven SaaS projects, connecting onboarding, roadmaps, resourcing, and go-live.
brief: Datava’s customers needed more than access to a data platform. Credit unions, banks, and manufacturers needed implementations that connected product capabilities with their operating workflows. Projects covered onboarding, CRM, data warehousing, incentives, referrals, loan pipelines, analytics, and reporting.
ownership: Manage ten engineers delivering data-driven SaaS through professional services.
Own a portfolio of client projects across the engagement lifecycle.
Coordinate stakeholder communication, project plans, engineering capacity, and customer-success scorecards.
delivery: I connected customer roadmaps with the engineering work needed to deliver them. That included lean product specifications, documentation, Kanban planning, QA, and go-live coordination. Regular meetings and explicit plans kept clients and delivery teams aligned on scope and progress.

Engineering leadership included mentoring, running standups, and triaging project resourcing. The customer-success scorecard provided a structured way to review each institution’s engagement alongside its active projects. The work joined delivery management with ongoing customer relationships.
outcomes: Maintained ownership across onboarding, implementation, and continuing customer engagement.
Coordinated a ten-engineer professional-services team across a broad set of product modules.
Connected project delivery, resource allocation, and customer-success reviews within the same operating process.
lesson: Adoption depends on delivery discipline. Roadmaps and product features become useful when customers understand the next step and the team has the capacity and specifications to deliver it.
image_alt: Datava portfolio slide showing customer-success responsibilities and financial-services product interfaces

title: Customer engineering at the edge.
summary: Worked across solutions, support, and full-stack engineering on a distributed platform for CDN, web security, and customer-facing infrastructure.
brief: Section operated a global platform for web performance and security. Customers depended on its delivery and protection layers during normal traffic, major campaigns, outages, and denial-of-service incidents. The role required moving between customer engineering, solutions engineering, support, and development.
ownership: Take difficult customer-facing technical issues through investigation and resolution.
Support onboarding, CDN configuration, bot management, and integration projects.
Contribute to dashboards, modules, internal specifications, runbooks, and public documentation.
delivery: The work combined direct customer communication with hands-on engineering. I handled incidents affecting major websites and helped resolve competing technical requirements across customer and platform teams. The portfolio names Toyota, Lexus, Coles, and BoxyCharm among the customer environments involved.

The technical stack included Sails.js, React, Grafana, Kibana, Kubernetes, Docker, Varnish, OpenResty, and Lua. Delivery spanned several infrastructure providers and a fully remote team. Zendesk, GitHub, Slack, and shared documentation supported the handoff between incident response, planned projects, and ongoing support.
outcomes: Delivered customer onboarding, configuration, and solution-engineering work alongside operational support.
Contributed engineering and documentation to the platform’s customer-facing delivery process.
Built experience translating high-pressure technical incidents into coordinated customer action.
lesson: Infrastructure customer success requires both technical depth and clear ownership. The customer needs someone who can understand the system, explain the next action, and stay with the problem.
image_alt: Section.io portfolio slide covering customer engineering, cloud infrastructure, and enterprise website delivery

title: Twelve domains. One coordinated launch plan.
summary: Documented and coordinated the onboarding of twelve Toyota and Lexus bare domains, including redirect logic and tests before and after launch.
brief: Toyota and Lexus required onboarding for twelve bare domains, including toyota.com, lexus.com, and toyotacertified.com. These addresses were important entry points for customers, including traffic generated by advertising. Redirect behavior needed to be explicit and coordinated across multiple business teams.
ownership: Write the product and support documentation for the domain applications.
Specify redirect logic, implementation options, and pre-launch and post-launch tests.
Work directly with Toyota project management and business teams through onboarding.
delivery: I documented an application for each domain, covering the redirection rules and the relevant technology choices, including Varnish and OpenResty. The Section product document became the shared source of truth for the onboarding work, giving the teams a common reference for implementation and validation.

Launches were coordinated during off-peak, out-of-hours windows. The work included straightforward bare-domain redirects as well as the more complex routing associated with the wider Toyota and Lexus domain portfolio. Explicit tests on both sides of go-live kept the intended behavior visible throughout the transition.
outcomes: Onboarded all twelve domains in coordination with Toyota’s teams.
Created product and support documentation used as the source of truth during onboarding.
Defined launch and validation steps for public-facing domain behavior.
lesson: A redirect can be a business-critical product surface. Treating domain behavior as a documented, testable release helps connect infrastructure changes with the customer journeys they affect.
image_alt: Toyota and Lexus portfolio slide describing twelve bare-domain redirectors and showing automotive website examples

title: Connecting product launches with systems operations.
summary: Coordinated software and systems teams across ACH payments, managed Wi-Fi, and broadband product delivery within Sonic’s Systems Operations Center.
brief: Sonic’s Systems Operations Center connected software development with the infrastructure behind customer services. The project portfolio included an ACH payments integration, an eero mesh Wi-Fi service, and the launch of an IP broadband product group. Each involved both product decisions and operational delivery.
ownership: Coordinate six full-stack developers and six systems administrators.
Manage product work for the ACH payments integration.
Manage projects for the eero Wi-Fi service and IP broadband product launch.
delivery: The role brought requirements, service design, and delivery planning into the same conversation. I worked across product and service design, design thinking, and UX/UI to connect customer-facing behavior with the supporting systems.

Planning used Jira with Scrum and Kanban alongside Waterfall projects. That mix reflected different delivery needs within the program. The central responsibility was coordination: helping software and systems specialists work toward shared product and launch objectives.
outcomes: Coordinated a twelve-person group spanning development and systems administration.
Owned product or project responsibilities across payments, Wi-Fi, and broadband initiatives.
Connected service design with the teams responsible for implementation and operations.
lesson: A service launch reaches beyond the application. Product ownership needs to connect user experience, payment behavior, infrastructure, and the teams that will operate the service.
image_alt: Sonic portfolio slide with broadband and Wi-Fi service screenshots and Systems Operations Center delivery responsibilities

title: Coordinating a public-comment campaign.
summary: Managed a digital advocacy project connecting executive direction, creative work, development, communications, and FCC-facing integration.
brief: Save Competition was a Sonic initiative involving FCC advocacy and direct email campaigns. The delivery challenge connected a public-facing campaign with internal executive, creative, engineering, and communications work, as well as an external regulatory interface.
ownership: Manage Agile development directly across the CEO, creative, developer, and communications teams.
Coordinate the digital campaign and its technical delivery.
Curate more than 9,000 citizen comments associated with the FCC campaign.
delivery: I worked as the programming project manager within Sonic, linking executive intent with the creative assets and development tasks needed for the campaign. The project combined campaign publishing and communication with a technical integration using Docker, AWS, and the FCC API.

The portfolio records the curation of more than 9,000 citizen comments. Content handling was therefore a substantial part of the project alongside the campaign experience and its technical integration.
outcomes: Coordinated a cross-functional public-facing campaign project.
Curated more than 9,000 citizen FCC comments.
Connected campaign delivery with a Docker/AWS implementation and FCC API integration.
lesson: Public-facing campaigns need the same delivery discipline as other digital products: explicit ownership, clear handoffs, and a reliable connection between communication and implementation.
image_alt: Save Competition portfolio slide with campaign website screenshots and a summary of FCC comment and integration work

title: Keeping public science information accessible and maintained.
summary: Managed a substantial public web estate while coordinating a mobile-first redesign, vendor delivery, content operations, and platform security maintenance.
brief: The California Institute for Regenerative Medicine needed ongoing stewardship of a large public web estate. The work combined Drupal and WordPress operations with a website refresh and mobile-first redesign. Content structure, vendor coordination, and code maintenance were all part of the role.
ownership: Manage content operations across more than 6,000 pages and fifteen content types.
Lead the search for a website refresh agency and manage vendor coordination.
Technically manage the redesign while maintaining code, documentation, and operational support.
delivery: I worked on landing pages, rich-content page building, and the technical delivery of the mobile-first redesign. The hosting and delivery environment included Acquia, Pantheon, Cloudflare CDN, and self-hosting. Product specifications and runbooks supported both planned changes and day-to-day operations.
Drupal code maintenance included responding to the vulnerability commonly known as Drupalgeddon. The portfolio records successful defensive maintenance during that period.
outcomes: Maintained a public content estate of more than 6,000 pages with fifteen content types.
Coordinated the technical and vendor work behind a mobile-first website redesign.
Combined publishing support with documented operations and security maintenance.
lesson: A public website is an ongoing service. Redesign work is strongest when content ownership, maintainable publishing patterns, vendor accountability, and security operations are addressed together.
image_alt: California Institute for Regenerative Medicine portfolio slide with mobile and desktop website examples and content-management responsibilities

title: Three hospitality brands, one delivery program.
summary: Led the software delivery lifecycle for a multi-brand accommodation platform with a shared codebase and a substantial destination and room-content estate.
brief: Mantra Resorts’ accommodation ecommerce work spanned the Mantra, BreakFree, and Peppers domains. The platform combined a single codebase with three distinct brand destinations and approximately 10,000 unique destination and hotel-room content items.
ownership: Manage the full lifecycle from requirements and specification through acceptance, launch, and documentation.
Coordinate ten developers across a nine-month program.
Connect the multisite platform and custom module work with the accommodation ecommerce requirements.
delivery: The program covered requirements, specifications, task definition, development, testing, and acceptance before launch. The implementation used custom .NET/DotNetNuke modules and a shared codebase supporting the three domains.

The source slide records a nine-month delivery period, ten developers, and an AUD 500,000 project scale. The delivery sequence connected the shared platform with the destination and room content, testing, acceptance, and launch documentation.
outcomes: Delivered accommodation ecommerce work across three domains using one codebase.
Coordinated a substantial destination and hotel-room content estate with custom application development.
Owned the delivery sequence from requirements to launch and documentation.
lesson: A shared platform can support multiple brands when the common system and the brand-specific requirements are made explicit. Delivery leadership connects that architecture to content, acceptance, and launch.
image_alt: Mantra Resorts portfolio slide with Mantra, BreakFree, and Peppers website examples and the multisite ecommerce delivery scope

title: Enabling newsrooms to publish through change.
summary: Empowered publishing and business teams through major newspaper website upgrades, multimedia production, internal knowledge systems, and advertising integrations.
brief: Nationwide News combined continuing web publishing operations with major changes to newspaper websites and internal systems. The portfolio highlights four major upgrades across The Australian and The Daily Telegraph, alongside advertising, editorial, knowledge-management, and subscription work.
ownership: Act as an internal web resource across major upgrades, ongoing operations, consulting, and projects.
Enable editorial and advertising teams through multimedia production, integrations, prototypes, and content operations.
Coordinate external vendors, including Microsoft Consulting, alongside internal stakeholders.
delivery: The work included SharePoint intranet and knowledge-management projects, plus OpenVMS mainframe API integrations for business-to-business advertising and news workflows. Product designs, prototypes, and proofs of concept explored the next generation of advertising and editorial tools.

I also produced web video and multimedia editorial during major breaking-news periods, including 9/11 and the Iraq War. Omnichannel subscription campaigns and everyday content operations ran alongside platform changes. The role connected the pace of publishing with the implementation work needed to keep evolving the web estate.
outcomes: Contributed as an internal web resource across four major newspaper website upgrades.
Enabled multimedia publishing during major breaking-news events.
Connected editorial, advertising, internal knowledge systems, and vendor-led projects through hands-on web delivery.
lesson: Publishing transformation depends on enabling the people who publish. The systems must evolve while editorial and commercial teams continue doing time-sensitive work.

title: Let’s build what comes next.
summary: Based in the San Francisco Bay Area, with experience connecting technology delivery, customer success, and business operations across Australia and the United States.
brief: The final portfolio slide brings the work back to a conversation. I’m interested in hands-on technology leadership where product development, engineering, and operations are connected to the needs of a growing business.
ownership: Turn a business objective into a practical delivery plan.
Lead the cross-functional teams that build, launch, and operate the product.
Stay close to the implementation, the customer experience, and the people doing the work.
delivery: The case studies show the kinds of challenges I have worked on: commerce migration, data-platform adoption, customer-facing infrastructure, service launches, and public web publishing. They are starting points for discussing your operating context and the change you need to make.

Email is the simplest way to begin. Share a short description of the business, the role or project, and the constraint you want to solve. My LinkedIn profile and downloadable resume provide additional professional context.
outcomes: Review a specific case study together to discuss relevant experience.
Connect the next business objective with the people, systems, and delivery work it requires.
lesson: I build products that customers buy and people love, and lead the cross-functional teams that do it.
